Apps I built .
Eight apps, from a Chrome extension to a full video editor.
All apps →
Tuck
Chrome extension
Every extension you have installed, in one popup, each with its own switch. Search them, or file them into folders you name. Turn the whole lot off in one click, and lock the ones you cannot work without so they survive it.
Add to Chrome ↗
Recall
macOS app
Save a workspace once. The apps, the files, the Chrome profile, and the slot on screen where each window belongs. Open it tomorrow and the whole desk comes back the way you left it, down to which half of the screen each window was using.
See it on the Apps page →
Refill
macOS menu bar
How much Claude you have left, live in the menu bar. Both windows, the five-hour and the seven-day, each with its own reset clock. You see the limit coming. The check itself costs no quota.
See it on the Apps page →
Frost
Chrome extension
Puts tabs you have not touched in a while to sleep, using Chrome's own discard. A sixty-tab window stops costing what a sixty-tab window costs. Every sleeping tab keeps its address, its title and its full back history, so waking one is just the page loading again.
See it on the Apps page →
Cropper
macOS app
A video editor that runs on your own Mac. Drop a video in and it transcribes every word. Then it lists the dead pauses, the filler words and the takes you said twice, each one quoted back to you. Tick what to lose and it renders the MP4. No account, no watermark, no length limit.
See it on the Apps page →
TITIS
macOS app
One hotkey reads whatever text you have highlighted, in any app on your Mac. It works out whether the selection is English or Czech, then switches to the best voice you have installed for that language. The speech is made on your machine, so nothing is sent anywhere.
See it on the Apps page →
OWCO
Web app
Give it your website and it reads back through your own pages, looking for what you still claim that is no longer true. A number that moved. A promise the homepage makes that page four contradicts. Each finding comes back with the exact words, why it is wrong now, and the page it was checked against.
Try the scan ↗
Nexus
Off-Plate tool
Point it at a business and it works through the public record: the Google profile, the website, the socials, the Czech business registers, and whether AI assistants name the place at all when a customer asks. It returns one card. The clearest measurable problem, who can approve fixing it, and a lawful way to reach them.
Open Nexus ↗
What using it is really like .
A first draft comes together in minutes and that part feels like magic. Then the real work starts: the checking, the fixing and the small calls only you can make. Most of the time goes there, and none of it gets automated. The shortcuts on this site are for the fast part.
Minutes to a first draft that looks finished
Hours to make it actually true
0 of that part gets automated
Small tools that do the math for you .
Calculators and checkers that run in your browser: what a month of AI costs, whether your text fits, when a task is worth automating.

## Your first hour with AI
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/start

Michael’s
Corner .
Home Start here Prompt library Tools Apps I built Videos Who I am
Menu
Get the kit →
Your first hour with AI .
Everything below came from people describing what they got wrong first. Tick it off as you go. Your ticks are saved on this device, so you can close the tab and come back.
The checklist
0 of 20 done
Before you type anything
Start with a job already on your desk, not a test question
Know what it is bad at first: live prices, exact arithmetic, slide decks
Tried it years ago and wrote it off? That verdict is out of date
For one week, note anything you do more than twice. That is your real list
How to ask
Paste the actual material. It is strong on what you bring, weak on what it recalls
Say who you are, what you want out of it, and what you already tried
Ask what it needs from you before you ask it for the work
For anything long, make it plan first and write second
Do not describe your tone. Paste two paragraphs you wrote and say match this
Tell it which words and habits you do not want back
Before you trust a word of it
Check every number, date, price and name before you use it
Do the arithmetic yourself. It gets sums wrong in a confident voice
For research, give it the source and say to answer only from that
Ask what it is unsure about. That question gets a straighter answer
Push back on the first answer. It is built to agree with you
Never send its writing out untouched. People recognise it now
Stop it forgetting you
Put your standing context in custom instructions or a project
One chat per topic. When a long one starts drifting, start a fresh one
Find the model picker. The default is not always the right one
Stay on the free version until you hit a wall you can name
0 of 20 done
Not sure what to bring .
The advice to start with a real task is useless if you do not yet know what it is for. So here are six you almost certainly have lying around.
The message you keep not sending
A reply you owe, a price rise, a no. Paste the thread you are replying to.
The document you have to read anyway
A contract, a report, a policy. Ask what it says and what to watch out for.
Notes that never became anything
Meeting scrawl, voice-note dumps, half a plan. Ask for the shape hiding in them.
A decision you keep circling
Lay out the options, ask what you have not considered, then argue with the answer.
Something you nodded along to
A word or an idea you pretended to understand. Ask for it in plain language.
A form or an application
A grant, a claim, a listing. Give it the rules and your facts, and make it find the gaps.
Your first hour, step by step .
01
Pick one tool
ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, and the free version is fine. Do not spend your first hour comparing them. For everything on this page they are close enough. Pick one and stay with it for a week, because the skill you are building transfers and the tool comparison does not.
02
Bring something off your own desk
Not "write me a poem." Something you already owe someone this week. If nothing comes to mind, take one off the list above. The people who quit are almost always the ones who tested it on a party trick and judged it on that.
03
Hand over the material
This is the whole game. It is strong on what you give it and weak on what it has to remember, so paste the email, the document, the notes, the numbers. Then say who you are, what you want out of it, and what you already tried.
04
Make it ask you first
Before you ask for the work, ask what it needs from you to do the work well. Ten seconds of that beats twenty minutes spent polishing an answer built on a guess. For anything long, have it plan first and write second.
05
Check it, then push back
It writes a wrong answer as confidently as a right one, so every number, date, price and name gets checked before you use it. Then argue with it. The first draft is a draft, and it is built to agree with you.
06
Stop retyping yourself
If you explain your job at the start of every chat, put that somewhere permanent instead: custom instructions, or a project. One chat per topic, and when a long one starts drifting, begin a fresh one with a summary.
That is the hour .
When you want prompts already written this way, the library is next door. Eighty of them, in ten packs.

## Who I am
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/about

Michael’s
Corner .
Home Start here Prompt library Tools Apps I built Videos Who I am
Menu
Get the kit →
Not a developer.
I build anyway .
I am Michael. A normal day job, and more than twenty finished projects on the side.
What I got good at
Describing what I want yes
Pushing back on a wrong answer yes
Doing the part it will not do yes
Writing code no
Where to find me
mihael.florian@gmail.com
Watch
Apps
I am not a developer. I have a normal day job, and I build things with AI anyway.
The list so far includes a finance app that tracks my debts and my budget, a training site with a 3D wireframe figure I could never have coded myself, a road-trip planner with maps and expense splitting that four of us used on a real holiday in Italy, two Chrome extensions, a small tool that turns one sentence into a Spotify playlist, and this website.
None of that made me an engineer. What I got good at is different: describing what I want clearly, pushing back when the answer is wrong, and doing the hands-on work a tool will not do for you. Most of what I put here comes straight out of that, the prompts I lean on and the small tools I built.
I take what has worked for me and write it down here .
Two years in, I still have the same day job. I just get more done in the time I have. Take whatever is useful, and let me know how it goes.
20+ projects built, one day job
2 yrs of doing this every week
0 lines of code I could write before
1 day job, still

## Michael's AI Starter Kit
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/kit

Michael’s
Corner .
Home Start here Prompt library Tools Apps I built Videos Who I am
Menu
Get the kit →
Michael’s AI Starter Kit .
Everything I would hand a friend who is starting with AI this week. The full list is below, so you know exactly what you trade your email for.
Packing slip 6 items
01 The 10 prompts I actually reuse
Copied from my own library, paste-ready, with a note on when each one helps.
02 The plain-words model guide
Which AI to pick for which kind of job, explained without benchmark charts.
03 The first-hour walkthrough
Account, settings, and your first real task, in the order I would do them with you.
04 The cost cheat sheet
What the main tools cost per month, what the free versions cover, and when paying starts to make sense.
05 The “is this an AI job?” checklist
One page that tells you whether a task is worth handing to AI at all.
06 The fix-it lines
The short follow-up sentences I use when an answer is almost right.
This kit, all six items the paid vault, later
Send me the kit .
There is no signup form behind this yet. Email me and I reply with the kit. One click below fills in the subject for you.
Email me for the kit →
I reply by hand, usually within a day.
No form
No list
No countdown
No upsell at the end
Your address is used for the kit and my occasional emails, never sold, never shared. When the proper list is ready you will be the first on it, and every email will have an unsubscribe link.
The kit never expires and never gets taken back. After it, I write when I actually have something useful, which is closer to twice a month than twice a day.

AI cost calculator
Drag three sliders, see what a month of AI actually costs, on rates you can edit. Pure arithmetic. Every constant is visible and yours to change.

Words it writes back 300

Cost per month
$0.00
&#8776; 0 K&#269;
Copy as text
Share
How to read this number
This is a guide, not a bill. It multiplies your words by an estimate of tokens, then by the per-token rate you see above. Rates move, so they are yours to edit. The K&#269; line uses the exchange rate in the assumptions.
Under twenty dollars a month usually means the API beats a fixed subscription. Above that, run the breakeven tool before you pick.

## AI-slop detector
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/tools/ai-slop-detector

Skip to content
Michaels
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
All tools
AI-slop detector
Paste any text. A public list of pattern rules counts the AI tells and stamps a slop score, with every flagged line shown. It counts the habits AI text leans on. It cannot prove who wrote it.
Paste your text
0 words
Try it on a slop sample
Slop score
0
paste text to score it
Copy report
View all rules
What the score means
The score is hand-tuned so raw chatbot marketing copy lands above 60 and edited human copy lands under 20. It is a density measure: tells per word, floored so a two-line paste cannot spike. Every rule that ran is listed above, so the page cannot lie about what it counted.
A high score is not proof of anything. It means the text leans on patterns AI over-produces. Fix the flagged lines and the number drops.

Why a builder, not a generator
The expensive work in a hard email is translation: turning what happened into words that get the outcome without burning the relationship. This tool does the structure. Your AI writes the draft from your facts. You read it and decide to send.
Nothing is generated on this page. Every line in the prompt came from an input you can see.

## Fits-in-context checker
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/tools/fits-in-context

Skip to content
Michaels
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
All tools
Fits-in-context checker
Paste your document, learn instantly whether it fits a model's context window or needs splitting. The paste never leaves this page.
Paste your text
0 characters / &#8776; 0 words / &#8776; 0 tokens
Chars per token 4.0
Czech text? Use 3.
Answer reserve 30%
Room kept for the system prompt and the model's reply.
Your model's window (optional)
tokens
Estimated tokens
0
paste something to begin
Paste something first.
Copy as text
Share
How to read this number
The character count is exact. The token estimate is characters divided by the chars-per-token figure you set, so it is a rough guide by design, not a promise. A window has to hold your text plus the reply, which is why some room is reserved.
FITS means comfortable room. TIGHT means it squeezes in but risks truncation. SPLIT means break it into the number of parts shown.

## Prompt tightener
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/tools/prompt-tightener

Skip to content
Michaels
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
All tools
Prompt tightener
Paste a rambling prompt. It strips the filler it can prove is filler, flags the vague asks it cannot fix for you, and shows the word count drop. Deletion only. It never rewrites or adds a word.
Paste your prompt
0 words
Show changes (strike removed words)
Load a rambling example
Tightened prompt
Copy tightened prompt ↗
Copy report
Why deletion, not rewriting
If a tool rewrites your prompt, your meaning can drift and you would not notice. This one only removes exact filler phrases from a published list. Anything it is unsure about becomes a flag for you, not an edit. Text inside quotes or backticks is left alone.
A tight prompt is not a shorter prompt for its own sake. It is one where every word is doing a job.

## Should you automate it?
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/tools/should-you-automate

Skip to content
Michaels
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
All tools
Should you automate it?
Six honest questions about the task, one stamped verdict: automate now, assist only, or leave it human. The weights are published and the opinion is the product.
Score it →
6 of 6 left
Score
/
answer all six, then score
No verdict yet.
Copy as text
Share
How the score works
Each answer scores 0, 1 or 2, weighted by how much it matters. Frequency and whether the task is rules or judgment carry the most weight, because those decide whether a machine can follow it at all.
Three hard rules can override the score: a judgment call with expensive mistakes stays human, sensitive data caps you at assist-only, and rare tasks with slow setup never pay back. Those are not negotiable.

How to read this number
The API cost uses the same math as the cost calculator, against the subscription price you type. If they land within twenty percent of each other, price alone should not decide it.
Plans bundle app features and rate limits. The API needs an app to live in. Price is one input, not the whole answer.

## Best prompts for beginners
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/packs/beginners

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Best prompts for beginners
The prompts to learn first, for anyone who has heard of AI but never really used it. None of them need any setup. Copy one, fill in the brackets, paste it in.
01
Make it ask before it answers
Use this first, on anything that matters. It is the habit that separates people who get useful answers from people who get generic ones.
→
02
Rewrite my question before you answer it
Use this when you can feel that your question is vague but you are not sure how to sharpen it.
→
03
Answer only from what I gave you
Use this whenever the answer has to be right: a contract, a policy, a report, anything you would be embarrassed to get wrong.
→
04
Show me what you assumed
Use this on the answer you just got, before you act on any of it.
→
05
Explain it like I am new
Use this when someone used a word or an idea you did not follow and you would rather not pretend you did.
→
06
Say my request back to me
Use this before a long job, when you want to catch a misunderstanding while it is still cheap.
→
07
Break down the thing I keep avoiding
Use this on the task that has been moving down your list all week.
→
08
Work out what to hand over
Use this in your first week, once you have a rough sense of what it can do.
→

## Job hunting
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/packs/jobs

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .

Apps I built

Job hunting
Tailoring a CV to one specific posting is the job people reach for AI to do most often. It is also where it most often writes in things you never did. Every prompt here is built to stop that.
01
Tailor my CV to this one posting
Use this per application. It is the twenty minutes of rewriting you do for every job, done in two.
→
02
What is this posting actually asking for
Use this before you decide whether to apply at all.
→
03
Where am I genuinely under-qualified
Use this when you are torn about applying and want a straight answer rather than encouragement.
→
04
Turn my duties into results
Use this when your CV reads like a job description and you know it.
→
05
A note instead of a cover letter
Use this when a cover letter is expected but you know the usual template reads as filler.
→
06
Read this as a tired recruiter
Use this on your finished application, before you send it.
→
07
Rehearse the interview for this job
Use this the evening before, out loud if you can.
→
08
Reply to silence, and to a low offer
Use this when you are staring at the message box, rewriting the first line for the fifth time.
→

## Study smarter
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/packs/study

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Study smarter
For students at any level. The pattern that keeps coming up from people who actually learn this way is the same: make it test you instead of summarising for you, then make it explain what you got wrong.
01
Quiz me from my own notes
Use this instead of rereading. Rereading feels like studying and is mostly not.
→
02
Test me until I get one wrong
Use this when you think you know a topic and want to find out whether you do.
→
03
Why did I get this wrong
Use this on a returned test or practice paper, on the questions you lost marks on.
→
04
Let me explain it and find my holes
Use this when you can follow the material while reading but cannot reproduce it afterwards.
→
05
Decode a paragraph I cannot get through
Use this on dense academic reading, when you have read the same three lines four times.
→
06
Turn this into flashcards
Use this when card-making is eating the time you meant to spend studying.
→
07
Am I actually ready for this exam
Use this a week out, when you want a real answer instead of a feeling.
→
08
Plan the week before the exam
Use this when you know what is coming and have no idea how to fit it in.
→

## Sounding like a human
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/packs/human

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am

&#8592; Back to all prompts
Sounding like a human
People spot AI writing now, and they think less of you for sending it. These strip the tells, keep your own voice, and cut the padding that gets added when you ask for something to be made better.
01
Write in my voice, from samples
Use this instead of asking for a friendly tone. Adjectives make it guess, examples do not.
→
02
Strip the AI tells out of this
Use this on anything generated that you are about to put your name on.
→
03
Cut this in half
Use this on anything that felt long while you were writing it.
→
04
Would this get read as AI, and why
Use this when something you wrote yourself has started to feel machine written to you.
→
05
Fix my grammar and nothing else
Use this when you want the errors gone but the writing left alone.
→
06
Same message, three readers
Use this when the same news has to go to your boss, your team and a client.
→
07
Take the corporate out of this
Use this when your own draft has gone stiff and you cannot hear it any more.
→
08
Titles that are not clickbait
Use this when you need a subject line, a heading or a title and every option sounds either dull or oversold.
→

Running a small business
For people running a small business on their own or with a few staff. Owners rarely say the tools are bad. They say they never knew what to actually type. These are the things worth typing.
01
Read my website as a sceptical customer
Use this when your site has been the same for a year and you can no longer see it.
→
02
A month of posts for my business
Use this when the social account has gone quiet again and you need a run of things to say.
→
03
Second opinion on a real decision
Use this on an actual business decision, the kind that has been on your mind for a fortnight.
→
04
Follow up on the quote they never answered
Use this on the quote you sent two weeks ago that has been sitting there since.
→
05
Price this without underselling it
Use this when you catch yourself about to quote low because you are afraid of the silence.
→
06
Turn my job notes into something a customer can read
Use this at the end of a job, when your notes are scribble and the customer wants an update.
→
07
The one-pager I leave behind
Use this once, then reuse it for every job of the same kind.
→
08
Ten questions about my own business
Use this when things are fine but you have a feeling something is off and cannot name it.
→

## Getting found by AI
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/packs/found

Skip to content
Skip to content

Getting found by AI
People now ask an assistant for a recommendation the way they used to search. This pack checks what it says about you and finds where the wrong answer comes from. A word of warning: being mentioned is not the same as being hired, and anyone selling you a mention count is selling a vanity number.
01
What does it say about my business
Use this first. Run it in two or three different assistants, because they will not agree.
→
02
Find the facts that are out of date
Use this after the first prompt, on anything it got wrong.
→
03
Who gets recommended instead of me
Use this when the assistant names competitors and you want to know what they have that you do not.
→
04
The twenty questions my customers actually ask
Use this to find out what you should have a clear answer to on your site.
→
05
Write the who this is not for section
Use this when you are trying to be right for everyone and ending up specific to nobody.
→
06
Turn my services into plain answerable facts
Use this on service pages that describe what you do without ever quite saying it.
→
07
An FAQ from questions people really asked
Use this when you have a pile of enquiry emails and no FAQ.
→
08
Does my page answer before it sells
Use this on any page you expect a stranger to land on.
→

Awkward work messages
The messages you rewrite five times and still do not send. Saying no, chasing for the third time, disagreeing with your manager, delivering news nobody wants. Each of these keeps your facts and fixes only the wording.
01
Make this professionally neutral
Use this when what you wrote is accurate but says out loud what you actually think of someone.
→
02
Say no without burning it
Use this on the request you should decline and have been avoiding for three days.
→
03
Chase without nagging
Use this on the third follow-up, when polite is starting to feel like a lie.
→
04
Deliver the bad news
Use this on the message you keep starting and deleting.
→
05
Push back on my manager, in writing
Use this when you think a decision is wrong and it needs to be on record.
→
06
Forty minutes of meeting into five lines
Use this straight after the call, while you still remember who meant what.
→
07
Write feedback that is specific, not personal
Use this before a review conversation you are dreading.
→
08
The version I can actually send
Use this when you have written the honest reply and know you must not send it.
→

Freelance client handling
For people who are the whole business. The recurring theme from freelancers is the conversations around the work: quoting, scope creep, silence and chasing money. These are for those.
01
The client has gone quiet
Use this five days into silence, when you are not sure if you are being ignored or forgotten.
→
02
Talk me to a number before I lowball it
Use this before you send a price, especially if you have a habit of going in low.
→
03
This is out of scope, said kindly
Use this on the third small favour that was never in the agreement.
→
04
Turn their vague brief into a specification
Use this before you quote on anything described in a paragraph or less.
→
05
Chase the invoice
Use this when payment is overdue and you have started rehearsing the message in the shower.
→
06
The update they did not ask for
Use this mid-project, on a Friday, on anything running longer than a fortnight.
→
07
Rehearse the price conversation
Use this before a call where you have to say a number out loud.
→
08
Turn down the wrong project
Use this on the job you know you should not take and are talking yourself into.
→

## Money decisions
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/packs/money

Money decisions
Personal money, where a confident wrong answer costs you something real. Every prompt here forces it to work from your numbers and to show the arithmetic, because getting sums wrong in a certain voice is the thing it does most reliably.
01
Where is my money actually going
Use this when the month ends and you genuinely do not know where it went.
→
02
Which debt do I pay first
Use this when you have several and are paying a bit off each with no plan.
→
03
Second opinion on my plan
Use this when you have decided something and want it stress-tested before you act.
→
04
Compare these two options properly
Use this on any either-or with numbers: two insurance plans, two loans, buy against rent, two contracts.
→
05
What have I forgotten to count
Use this before committing to anything with an ongoing cost.
→
06
Explain this document in plain words
Use this on an insurance policy, a contract, a statement, anything you signed without fully reading.
→
07
Build a buffer from nothing
Use this when every unexpected bill becomes a small crisis.
→
08
Rehearse the money conversation
Use this before talking to a partner, a bank, or someone you owe.
→

Health and habits
Habits, food and follow-through. These do not replace a doctor and they will not know your body, so the prompts are built to make it question you rather than prescribe at you. Anything with a symptom in it belongs in front of a professional.
01
Ten questions to find what is really stopping me
Use this when you know what you should be doing and are somehow not doing it.
→
02
Meals from what is actually in the fridge
Use this at 6pm when you are about to order in for the third time this week.
→
03
The smallest version of this habit
Use this when you have started the same habit four times and quit it four times.
→
04
Sanity check something I read online
Use this on any confident health claim you saw on a video or a forum.
→
05
Why did I stop, without the lecture
Use this after a streak breaks, instead of starting again from scratch on Monday.
→
06
Turn a vague goal into a weekly plan
Use this when your goal is a feeling rather than something you could measure.
→
07
Check in on me honestly
Use this weekly, in the same chat, once a plan is running.
→
08
What would need to be true for this to work
Use this before starting something big, while quitting is still cheap.

## Make it ask before it answers
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/interview-me-first

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Make it ask before it answers
Use this first, on anything that matters. It is the habit that separates people who get useful answers from people who get generic ones.
What to fill in
[ describe what you want, roughly, in a sentence or two ]
The tip
Ten seconds of this beats twenty minutes spent fixing an answer built on a guess. If you take one prompt from this whole site, take this one.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
Start here
The prompt
copy target
I want help with this: [describe what you want, roughly, in a sentence or two].
Do not answer yet. First tell me what you would need to know to do this well, then ask me the three to five questions that would actually change your answer. Ask them one at a time and wait for my reply before the next one.
While you are interviewing me:
- Ask about things that would change what you produce. Skip background that would not.
- If an answer of mine is vague, push once for something concrete before moving on.
- Do not start solving it while we are still talking.
When you have enough, say "Ready" and give me your answer. If something is still missing, name it and say what you assumed instead of quietly guessing.
Copy prompt

## Rewrite my question before you answer it
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/fix-my-question

Michael’s
Corner .

Rewrite my question before you answer it

copy target

Break down the thing I keep avoiding
Use this on the task that has been moving down your list all week.
What to fill in
[ name the task, honestly ]
[ any detail, deadline, or reason it is stuck. If you do not know why it is stuck, say so. ]
The tip
The ten minute step is the point. If the first thing on the list still feels heavy, tell it to go smaller.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
Start here
The prompt
copy target

4. Tell me which step is the one I am really avoiding, and why you think so.
Keep it to one screen. No pep talk.

Use this in your first week, once you have a rough sense of what it can do.
What to fill in
[ list the things you do repeatedly, however roughly. Include the boring ones. ]

Tailor my CV to this one posting
Use this per application. It is the twenty minutes of rewriting you do for every job, done in two.
What to fill in
[ paste the whole posting, including the boring requirements section ]
[ paste your CV as it stands ]
The tip
Read every rewritten line before you send it. The quickest way to lose an interview is being asked about a skill the AI gave you.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For applicants
The prompt
copy target
Here is the job posting:
[paste the whole posting, including the boring requirements section]

- Where you reword a bullet, keep the fact and change only the framing.

A note instead of a cover letter
Use this when a cover letter is expected but you know the usual template reads as filler.
What to fill in
[ paste it ]
[ paste or summarise ]
[ one honest line. If the honest answer is that you need a job, write that and I will work with what is true. ]
The tip
Cover letters became easy to generate, so they became easy to spot. Short and specific now beats polished.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For applicants
The prompt
copy target

- End with a simple next step, not a flourish.

[ paste your lecture notes, chapter summary, or slides ]

## Test me until I get one wrong
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/test-until-i-fail

Skip to content
Skip to content

Corner .

Start here

Tools
Apps I built

Who I am

Test me until I get one wrong
Use this when you think you know a topic and want to find out whether you do.
What to fill in
[ name the topic ]
[ paste your notes, or say "use standard coverage of this topic" ]
The tip
The point is finding the edge of what you know. Getting everything right means the questions were too easy, so say so.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For students
The prompt
copy target
Topic: [name the topic]
My material: [paste your notes, or say "use standard coverage of this topic"]
Ask me progressively harder questions on this, one at a time, until I get one wrong.
When I get one wrong:
1. Stop the escalation.
2. Tell me what the gap actually is. Not just the right answer, the misunderstanding behind my wrong one.
3. Explain that specific gap.
4. Ask me two more questions on that same gap to check it has closed.
5. Then carry on getting harder.
If I am getting everything right, get harder faster.

[ paste it, or write "not given" ]

Wrong answers are more useful than right ones. The diagnosis of the mistake is the part that stops it happening again.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For students
The prompt
copy target
Here is the question: [paste it]
Here is my answer: [paste exactly what you wrote, mistakes included]
Here is the correct answer, if I have it: [paste it, or write "not given"]
Do not just tell me the right answer. Tell me:
1. What I appear to have misunderstood, based on what I actually wrote.
2. Whether this is a knowledge gap, a misread question, or a careless slip. Say which, and how you can tell.
3. What the general version of this mistake is, so I can spot it next time.
4. Two practice questions that would catch this same mistake again.
If my answer is closer to right than it looks, say that too.

Am I actually ready for this exam
Use this a week out, when you want a real answer instead of a feeling.
What to fill in
[ what it covers, the format, and the date ]
[ paste it ]
The tip
Testing the topics you feel best about is the useful bit. That is where the surprises are.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For students
The prompt
copy target
Exam: [what it covers, the format, and the date]
Syllabus or topic list: [paste it]

## Strip the AI tells out of this
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/strip-the-tells

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Strip the AI tells out of this
Use this on anything generated that you are about to put your name on.
What to fill in
[ paste it ]
The tip
The list at the end is the part that trains you. After a few runs you will start hearing the tells before you write them.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For writing
The prompt
copy target
Here is the text:
[paste it]
Remove the things that make it read as machine written:
- Em dashes. Use commas, full stops or a rewrite.
- The three-item list where all three items are the same shape.
- Openers like "In today's fast-paced world" and "It's important to note that".
- "Not just X, but Y" and every other manufactured contrast.
- Words like leverage, robust, seamless, delve, landscape, foster, underscore, testament.
- Sentences that all run to the same length.
- A closing line that restates the whole thing.
Keep every fact and every point. Change only how it sounds.
Then list what you removed, so I can see the pattern and stop writing it myself.
Copy prompt

Cut this in half
Use this on anything that felt long while you were writing it.
What to fill in
[ paste it ]
The tip
Ask for half even when you want a third off. Aiming at half and landing at 40% is better than aiming at 10% and cutting nothing.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For writing
The prompt
copy target
Here is my text:
[paste it]

Rules:

- Cut throat-clearing, restatement, and hedges like "I think that maybe we could possibly".

- Do not replace a long simple word with a short complicated one.
- Do not turn it into notes. It should still read as prose.

## Second opinion on a real decision
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/second-opinion

Skip to content

Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Second opinion on a real decision
Use this on an actual business decision, the kind that has been on your mind for a fortnight.
What to fill in
[ raise prices, hire versus outsource, sign a lease, add a service, drop a client. Say which. ]
[ the numbers, the constraints, the deadline. Include what you are unsure of. ]
[ and why ]
The tip
Answer its questions honestly, including the ones about numbers you have been avoiding looking at. That part is usually the actual blocker.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For owners
The prompt
copy target
The decision: [raise prices, hire versus outsource, sign a lease, add a service, drop a client. Say which.]
What I know: [the numbers, the constraints, the deadline. Include what you are unsure of.]
What I am leaning towards: [and why]
Do this:
1. Ask me the questions you need before you can have a view. Wait for my answers.
2. Then give me the strongest case for my leaning, and the strongest case against it.
3. Tell me what I appear to be assuming without evidence.
4. Tell me what would have to be true for the other option to be the right one.
5. Say what you would want to know that I do not seem to have.
Do not tell me it depends and stop there. Take a position, and say what would change it.
Copy prompt
Michael’s
Corner .
AI is my superpower. Not my replacement.

Price this without underselling it
Use this when you catch yourself about to quote low because you are afraid of the silence.
What to fill in
[ what it involves, in detail ]
[ including the parts you always forget, like revisions and admin ]
[ materials, subcontractors, anything you pay out ]
[ and how it usually feels afterwards ]
[ budget signals, urgency, how they found me ]
The tip

Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For owners
The prompt
copy target
The job: [what it involves, in detail]

What I know about this customer: [budget signals, urgency, how they found me]

1. Ask me anything you need to price this properly.
2. Walk me to a number, showing the working.
3. Tell me where I am likely underselling, based on what I said about how it usually feels afterwards.
4. Give me the sentence I say when I give them the number, and the sentence I say if they push back.
5. Tell me the walk-away number and how to say no politely.
Do not tell me to charge what I am worth. Give me a figure and the reasoning.

Use this when what you wrote is accurate but says out loud what you actually think of someone.
What to fill in

This pack

The prompt
copy target

Say no without burning it

What to fill in
[ paste the request ]
[ the real reason ]
[ the relationship, future work, my week ]
[ or "nothing" ]
The tip

## Deliver the bad news
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/deliver-bad-news

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Deliver the bad news
Use this on the message you keep starting and deleting.
What to fill in
[ the facts ]
[ and what it costs them ]
[ or am doing ]
[ if anything ]
The tip
Leading with the bad news feels wrong and reads as respect. Burying it in paragraph four is what people actually resent.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For office work
The prompt
copy target
What happened: [the facts]
Who I am telling: [and what it costs them]
What I did about it: [or am doing]
What I need from them: [if anything]
Write the message.
Rules:
- The bad news goes in the first two sentences. Do not bury it under context.
- No softening it into ambiguity. They must know exactly how bad it is.
- Own what is mine to own. Do not over-apologise for what is not.
- Facts, then what happens next, then what I need. In that order.
- No "I wanted to reach out" and no passive voice hiding who did what.
Then tell me the question they will ask first, so I can answer it before they have to.
Copy prompt
Michael’s
Corner .

## Push back on my manager, in writing
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/disagree-upward

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Push back on my manager, in writing
Use this when you think a decision is wrong and it needs to be on record.
What to fill in
[ what has been decided ]
[ your reasoning and any evidence ]
[ and what it would cost ]
[ new, established, already disagreed once about this ]
[ reconsideration, or my objection recorded, or a specific change ]
The tip
The last line is what makes disagreeing safe. Being clear you will follow the call is what earns you a hearing on the next one.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For office work
The prompt
copy target
The decision: [what has been decided]
Why I think it is wrong: [your reasoning and any evidence]
What I would do instead: [and what it would cost]
My standing here: [new, established, already disagreed once about this]
What I want: [reconsideration, or my objection recorded, or a specific change]
Write it.
Rules:
- Lead with the shared goal, not with the disagreement.
- Argue the decision, never the person who made it.
- Be concrete about the risk. No vague "concerns".
- Offer the alternative with its cost stated honestly, including that it may not be worth it.
- Make it easy for them to change course without losing face.
- End by making clear I will get behind the decision either way, if that is true.
Then tell me how this reads if they are already defensive.
Copy prompt
Michael’s
Corner .
AI is my superpower. Not my replacement.

## Forty minutes of meeting into five lines
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/meeting-to-actions

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Forty minutes of meeting into five lines
Use this straight after the call, while you still remember who meant what.
What to fill in
[ paste them, messy is fine ]
[ unassigned ]
[ no date ]
The tip
The [unassigned] markers are the point. Actions with nobody's name on them are the ones that quietly do not happen.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For office work
The prompt
copy target
Here are my notes or the transcript:
[paste them, messy is fine]
Give me:
1. What was decided. Decisions only, not discussion.
2. What is still open, and who is deciding it.
3. Actions: what, who, by when. If a name or a date was not actually said, write [unassigned] or [no date] rather than guessing.
4. Anything said that contradicts something else said.
Rules:
- Only what is in my notes.
- Do not turn a maybe into a commitment. If someone said they would try, write that they would try.
- Under one screen.
Copy prompt

## Write feedback that is specific, not personal
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/difficult-feedback

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Write feedback that is specific, not personal
Use this before a review conversation you are dreading.
What to fill in
[ their role and how we work together ]
[ describe it honestly, including how it makes you feel ]
[ what happened, when. If you have none, say so. ]
[ concretely ]
[ if anything ]
The tip
If you cannot supply an example, you are not ready to give the feedback. That is the useful thing this catches.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For office work
The prompt
copy target
Who: [their role and how we work together]
What needs to change: [describe it honestly, including how it makes you feel]
Specific examples: [what happened, when. If you have none, say so.]
What good would look like: [concretely]
What I have already said about this: [if anything]
Turn it into feedback I can actually give.
Rules:
- Behaviour and effect, never character. Not "careless", but what happened and what it caused.
- Every point needs an example. If I have not given you one, tell me to find one rather than writing a general criticism.
- Say what good looks like in terms they could act on tomorrow.
- Do not sandwich it in praise. Say the praise if it is true, separately.
- Give me the opening sentence, because that is the one I will fumble.
Copy prompt
Michael’s
Corner .

## The version I can actually send
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/angry-draft

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
The version I can actually send
Use this when you have written the honest reply and know you must not send it.
What to fill in
[ paste it, all of it ]
[ the facts, without the feelings ]
[ the outcome you want ]
The tip
Point 3 is why this is not just softening. The angry draft usually contains the real issue, and the polite rewrite tends to lose it.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For office work
The prompt
copy target
Here is what I want to send:
[paste it, all of it]
Here is what actually happened:
[the facts, without the feelings]
Here is what I need to happen next:
[the outcome you want]
Do three things:
1. Tell me what in my draft would damage this relationship, and what it would cost me.
2. Write the version that gets me the outcome I asked for.
3. Tell me what in my draft was a legitimate point that the calm version should keep, because I do not want to lose the substance along with the tone.
Do not tell me to calm down or wait a day. I know. Give me the message.
Copy prompt

## The client has gone quiet
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/client-gone-quiet

Skip to content
Skip to content

&#8592; Back to all prompts
The client has gone quiet
Use this five days into silence, when you are not sure if you are being ignored or forgotten.
What to fill in
[ who they are and what stage we are at ]
[ what was said, and how many days ago ]
[ an approval, a file, a decision, payment ]
[ and what it costs me or them ]
[ paste it ]
The tip
Silence is usually their chaos, not your work. Assuming the worst and going quiet back is how projects die that did not need to.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For solo operators
The prompt
copy target
The client: [who they are and what stage we are at]
Last contact: [what was said, and how many days ago]
What I am waiting for: [an approval, a file, a decision, payment]
What is blocked by it: [and what it costs me or them]
Here is the last message in the thread:
[paste it]
Write my follow-up.
Rules:
- Under 90 words.
- No "just following up" and no apology for writing.
- Say plainly what is waiting and what it holds up.
- Give them a one-tap reply: a date, a yes, or an honest "we have paused this".
- Do not offer a discount or extra work to restart the conversation.
Then write the version I send a week after that, if this one also gets nothing.
Copy prompt

## Talk me to a number before I lowball it
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/quote-this-job

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Talk me to a number before I lowball it
Use this before you send a price, especially if you have a habit of going in low.
What to fill in
[ what they want, in as much detail as you have ]
[ hours or days, honestly ]
[ revisions, meetings, admin, the last 10% that takes 30% of the time ]
[ and whether it felt right afterwards ]
[ budget signals, how they found me, how they talk about money ]
The tip
Include the parts you always forget. That list is usually the whole difference between a job that pays and one that does not.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For solo operators
The prompt
copy target
The job: [what they want, in as much detail as you have]
What I think it will take: [hours or days, honestly]
What I always forget to count: [revisions, meetings, admin, the last 10% that takes 30% of the time]
My usual rate or last similar quote: [and whether it felt right afterwards]
What I know about this client: [budget signals, how they found me, how they talk about money]
Do this:
1. Ask me what you still need to price it properly. Wait for my answers.
2. Give me a number with the working shown.
3. Tell me where I have probably underestimated, using what I said about what I forget.
4. Give me the exact sentence for delivering the number.
5. Give me my walk-away figure and the polite decline.
Do not tell me to value myself. Give me a figure and the reasoning behind it.
Copy prompt

## This is out of scope, said kindly
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/out-of-scope

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
This is out of scope, said kindly
Use this on the third small favour that was never in the agreement.
What to fill in
[ the original scope ]
[ the new request ]
[ time, and what it delays ]
[ be honest ]
[ to charge for it, to trade it against something, or to decline ]
[ price and timeline ]
The tip
The reset line is the important one. A single favour rarely hurts. The precedent that you always say yes does.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For solo operators
The prompt
copy target
What we agreed: [the original scope]
What they are now asking for: [the new request]
What it would actually cost me: [time, and what it delays]
How many times this has happened: [be honest]
What I want: [to charge for it, to trade it against something, or to decline]
Write my reply.
Rules:
- Do not make them feel caught out. Most scope creep is not deliberate.
- Say clearly that it sits outside what we agreed, and why that matters.
- Give them a real choice: add it for [price and timeline], swap it for something already in scope, or leave it for later.
- No passive aggression and no listing everything else I have already absorbed for free.
- If I have let several go already, give me one line that resets the pattern without relitigating them.
Copy prompt

## Turn their vague brief into a specification
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/brief-to-spec

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Turn their vague brief into a specification
Use this before you quote on anything described in a paragraph or less.
What to fill in
[ paste their brief, however thin ]
[ brackets ]
The tip
Point 2 is where projects go wrong. What the client assumed was obvious is never in the brief, and it is never what you assumed.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For solo operators
The prompt
copy target
Here is what the client sent me:
[paste their brief, however thin]
Turn it into something I could be held to.
1. List what they have actually specified.
2. List what they have implied but not stated, and mark each as an assumption I need confirmed.
3. List what is missing entirely and would change the price.
4. Write the questions I should send back, in the order that gets me the most useful answers first. No more than six.
5. Draft the scope paragraph I would put in the proposal, with [brackets] wherever an answer is still needed.
Do not fill any gap with a sensible default. That is how the argument starts later.
Copy prompt

Corner .

## Chase the invoice
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/chase-the-invoice

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Chase the invoice
Use this when payment is overdue and you have started rehearsing the message in the shower.
What to fill in
[ amount, number, date sent, date due ]
[ days ]
[ paste previous reminders, or say "none" ]
[ ongoing work, one-off, want to keep them or not ]
[ late fees, interest, whatever the agreement says ]
[ 1, 2 or 3 ]
The tip
Send stage 1 on day one overdue, not day fourteen. Chasing early is normal business and reads as organised, not aggressive.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For solo operators
The prompt
copy target
Invoice: [amount, number, date sent, date due]
How overdue: [days]
What I have sent already: [paste previous reminders, or say "none"]
The relationship: [ongoing work, one-off, want to keep them or not]
My terms: [late fees, interest, whatever the agreement says]
Write the message for stage [1, 2 or 3].
1 is a first friendly nudge. 2 is firm with the terms named. 3 is the last message before I stop work or escalate.
Rules:
- State the amount, the invoice number and the due date every time.
- No apology, no "sorry to be a pain".
- Make paying easy: restate the details rather than pointing at an attachment.
- At stage 2 and 3, name what happens next as a fact, not a threat.
- Never suggest a discount for prompt payment on an invoice that is already late.
Copy prompt
Michael’s
Corner .

The update they did not ask for
Use this mid-project, on a Friday, on anything running longer than a fortnight.
What to fill in
[ what it is and how long it runs ]
[ including anything behind or worrying you ]
[ or nothing ]
[ and whether they have asked ]
The tip
This is the cheapest thing on this page. Clients who hear from you unprompted do not chase, do not panic, and do not go quiet.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For solo operators
The prompt
copy target
The project: [what it is and how long it runs]
Where it actually stands: [including anything behind or worrying you]
What I need from them: [or nothing]
What they are probably wondering: [and whether they have asked]
Write a short update.
Rules:
- Under 150 words.
- Lead with where it stands against the plan, including bad news if there is any.
- Anything I need from them goes in its own line with a date.
- Do not pad it to look busy. If a quiet week was a quiet week, say so and why.
- No "circling back", no "touching base".

## Rehearse the price conversation
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/rehearse-the-price

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Rehearse the price conversation
Use this before a call where you have to say a number out loud.
What to fill in
[ the job and the price ]
[ the reasoning ]
[ the actual fear ]
The tip
Do this out loud. The price conversation goes badly because you have never said the number to anyone before.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For solo operators
The prompt
copy target
What I am quoting: [the job and the price]
How I arrived at it: [the reasoning]
What I am afraid they will say: [the actual fear]
Play the client. Be the difficult but realistic version: someone who likes the work, thinks the price is high, and is going to push.
Rules for you:
- Push back the way a real client does. "That is more than we budgeted", "what would it cost without X", "our last supplier charged half".
- Do not fold when I hold my ground, and do not become a caricature.
- After each of my answers, stay in character.
- When I say "stop", come out of character and tell me: where I discounted without being asked, where I over-explained, and the one line that would have ended the objection cleanly.
Start when I say go.

## Turn down the wrong project
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/decline-bad-fit

Turn down the wrong project
Use this on the job you know you should not take and are talking yourself into.
What to fill in
[ what they want ]
[ the honest reason. Wrong work, bad signals, no time, price too low. ]
[ referrals, the relationship, my reputation with whoever introduced us ]
[ name or none ]
The tip
The two questions at the start are worth answering properly. Sometimes the honest answer is that you are tired, not that the job is wrong.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
For solo operators
The prompt
copy target
The project: [what they want]
Why I should say no: [the honest reason. Wrong work, bad signals, no time, price too low.]
What I would want to preserve: [referrals, the relationship, my reputation with whoever introduced us]
Whether there is anyone I would refer them to: [name or none]
First, challenge me. Ask me two questions to check I am turning it down for the right reason and not out of fear or a bad week.
Then write the decline.
Rules:
- Clear no, early in the message.
- One honest reason, without a lecture about their budget or their brief.
- Refer them on if I named someone.
- Leave the door open only if I actually want them back.
- Under 100 words.

## Where is my money actually going
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/where-money-goes

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Where is my money actually going
Use this when the month ends and you genuinely do not know where it went.
What to fill in
[ paste your transactions, or a rough list. Bank exports work fine. ]
The tip
Check the totals yourself. Adding up a list is exactly the kind of thing it does confidently and sometimes wrongly, so the visible arithmetic is not optional.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
Personal
The prompt
copy target
Here is a month of my spending:
[paste your transactions, or a rough list. Bank exports work fine.]
Do this:
1. Group it into categories that reflect how I actually live, not standard budget headings.
2. Show what each category came to and what share of the total it was.
3. Point out anything that surprised you about the shape of it.
4. Separate what is fixed and hard to change from what is genuinely discretionary.
5. Flag anything that looks like a subscription I may have forgotten.
Rules:
- Add up only what I gave you. Show your arithmetic for each category total so I can check it.
- If a transaction is ambiguous, ask rather than filing it somewhere.
- Do not tell me what to cut yet, and do not comment on my choices. Just show me the shape.
Copy prompt

## Which debt do I pay first
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/which-debt-first

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Which debt do I pay first
Use this when you have several and are paying a bit off each with no plan.
What to fill in
[ for each one: what it is, the balance, the interest rate, the minimum payment, and any fees or deadlines ]
[ amount ]
The tip
Both orders are valid. Cheapest on paper is worthless if you abandon it in month three, so pick the one you will actually finish.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
Personal
The prompt
copy target
Here is every debt I have:
[for each one: what it is, the balance, the interest rate, the minimum payment, and any fees or deadlines]
What I can put towards debt each month, beyond the minimums: [amount]
Do this:
1. Order them for paying off by cost, highest interest first, and show the total interest that path costs.
2. Order them smallest balance first, and show what that path costs.
3. Show the difference between the two in money and in months.
4. Say which you would pick and why, and be explicit that the second path costs more but is easier to stick to.
5. Flag anything with a deadline, a penalty or a rate that is about to change, since those may outrank both orders.
Show the arithmetic. If I have left out a rate you need, ask instead of assuming one.
Copy prompt
Michael’s
Corner .
AI is my superpower. Not my replacement.

## Second opinion on my plan

Second opinion on my plan
Use this when you have decided something and want it stress-tested before you act.
What to fill in
[ describe it, with the numbers ]
[ income, obligations, what a bad month looks like ]
[ list what you are taking for granted ]
The tip
Point 4 catches most people. Annual and irregular costs are what turn a plan that works on paper into one that fails in March.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
Personal
The prompt
copy target
Here is my plan: [describe it, with the numbers]
Here is my situation: [income, obligations, what a bad month looks like]
Here is what I am assuming: [list what you are taking for granted]
Do this:
1. List every assumption you can see in my plan, including the ones I did not name.
2. For each, say what happens to the plan if it turns out wrong.
3. Tell me which single assumption breaking would hurt most.
4. Tell me what I have not accounted for. Irregular costs, annual bills, the things that only show up once a year.
5. Say what you would want to know that I have not told you.
Do not reassure me. If the plan is fragile, say where.

What have I forgotten to count
Use this before committing to anything with an ongoing cost.
What to fill in
[ the thing ]
[ what you think it costs ]
[ what you included ]
The tip
The annual costs are the trap. Anything budgeted monthly quietly ignores the bills that arrive once a year, and those are the ones that break the month.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
Personal
The prompt
copy target
What I am about to commit to: [the thing]
The cost I have budgeted: [what you think it costs]
How I worked that out: [what you included]
Tell me what I have left out.
1. Costs that appear later: setup, insurance, maintenance, renewal, the thing that always needs replacing.
2. Costs that appear annually rather than monthly, which people forget when they budget in months.
3. What it stops me doing, in money terms.
4. What happens to the cost if my circumstances change in the obvious ways.
For each, say whether it is certain, likely or possible. Do not invent figures for my country or my situation. Where a number depends on where I am or who I am, ask me.

Build a buffer from nothing

What to fill in
[ income, when it arrives, how regular it is ]
[ including if it is nothing ]

Rehearse the money conversation
Use this before talking to a partner, a bank, or someone you owe.
What to fill in
[ and what our relationship is ]
[ the honest version, including anything I have been hiding or delaying ]
[ the outcome ]
[ the real fear ]
The tip
Lead with the number. Every version of this conversation that starts with context and works up to the figure goes worse than the one that starts with the figure.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
Personal
The prompt
copy target
Who I am talking to: [and what our relationship is]
What I need to say: [the honest version, including anything I have been hiding or delaying]
What I want out of it: [the outcome]
What I am afraid of: [the real fear]

## Ten questions to find what is really stopping me
URL: https://michaels-corner.netlify.app/prompts/ten-questions-constraint

Skip to content
Skip to content
Michael’s
Corner .
Home
Start here
Prompt library
Tools
Apps I built
Videos
Who I am
Get the kit →
&#8592; Back to all prompts
Ten questions to find what is really stopping me
Use this when you know what you should be doing and are somehow not doing it.
What to fill in
[ the goal ]
[ honestly ]
[ and how each one ended ]
The tip
The questions about circumstances are the ones that land. Most stuck habits are a logistics problem wearing a motivation costume.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
Personal
The prompt
copy target
What I am trying to do: [the goal]
How long I have been trying: [honestly]
What I have already tried: [and how each one ended]
Ask me ten questions, one at a time, to find the constraint I cannot see. Wait for each answer before the next.
Rules for your questions:
- Ask about what actually happened, not about what I intend.
- If an answer sounds rehearsed or too quick, follow it rather than moving on.
- At least three should be about my circumstances rather than my motivation. Time, money, other people, sleep.
- Do not give advice while we are still going.
At the end: tell me what you think is really in the way, quote the answers that led you there, and name the smallest change that would test it.

The smallest version of this habit

[ what you attempted, and where each attempt died ]
[ when you are free, when you are wrecked, what is fixed ]

ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini

The prompt
copy target

4. Tell me what to do on the day I miss it, because I will.
5. Tell me what to look at in four weeks to decide whether to make it bigger.
Do not motivate me. Give me the smallest thing and where it goes.

Why did I stop, without the lecture

What to fill in
[ the habit and how long it ran ]

Turn a vague goal into a weekly plan
Use this when your goal is a feeling rather than something you could measure.
What to fill in
[ say it however vague. "Get fitter", "eat better", "sleep properly" are all fine. ]
[ the real reason ]
[ honestly, with any numbers you have ]
[ time per week, equipment, money, and who else this has to fit around ]

Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
Personal
The prompt
copy target

3. Give me the weekly plan that fits the time I actually have, not an ideal week.
4. Tell me the leading indicator to watch, the thing that moves before the goal does.

Check in on me honestly
Use this weekly, in the same chat, once a plan is running.
What to fill in
[ paste your plan ]
The tip
Run it in the same conversation each week so it can see the pattern. One week is noise, four weeks is information.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
Personal
The prompt
copy target
Here is what I said I would do this week:
[paste your plan]
Ask me what actually happened, one question at a time.
Rules:
- Ask about what I did, not how I feel about what I did.
- If I am vague, ask again more specifically. "Most days" is not an answer.
- Do not congratulate me for a plan I did not follow.
- Do not scold me either. I want a straight record, not a mood.
- If I missed things, ask what was happening rather than why I did not push through.

## What would need to be true for this to work

What would need to be true for this to work
Use this before starting something big, while quitting is still cheap.
What to fill in
[ the plan ]
[ including the things you have not said out loud ]
[ and where that estimate comes from ]
The tip
The cheap test in point 5 is the whole value. Most big plans rest on one assumption you could check in an afternoon.
Works in
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini
This pack
Personal
The prompt
copy target
What I am about to start: [the plan]
What I am assuming will happen: [including the things you have not said out loud]
How long I expect it to take: [and where that estimate comes from]
Do this:

2. Mark each as within my control, partly in my control, or not in my control at all.

4. Tell me what the plan looks like if that one does fail, and whether it is still worth doing.
5. Tell me the cheapest test I could run this week to find out about the riskiest assumption before I commit.
Be blunt. I would rather hear it now.
